newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Tempers cool as Austria crisis talks drag on.
newsitem.headline: Tempers cool as Austria crisis talks drag on.

text.p: Crisis talks involving leaders of Austria's shaky coalition stretched into the night as the government made a last-ditch effort to patch up a bitter rift over the privatisation of the country's second biggest bank.

Chancellor Franz Vranitzky's Social Democrats and the conservative People's Party led by Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel are at loggerheads over the selloff of the prestigious Creditanstalt-Bankverein.

But as the time ticked on past midnight on Saturday, there was no sign of an imminent compromise, though Vranitzky's spokesman, Karl Krammer, said tempers had cooled during more than 10 hours of talks.
"We will continue the talks tonight, we will continue the talks tomorrow, we will continue day and night," a source close to the talks told reporters.
Political sources said the negotiations centred on 10 points proposed by Schuessel's party over the sale of Creditanstalt, long considered a conservative fiefdom.
The Social Democrats want Creditanstalt to be sold to Bank Austria, which is indirectly controlled by the Social Democrat-run City of Vienna.
Schuessel's conservatives, fighting to stop the Social Democrats dominating the banking industry, back a bid made by an international consortium led by Italian-controlled insurer EA-Generali.

Finance Minister Viktor Klima, a Social Democrat, has said he intends to award the tender to the highest bidder before Tuesday ahead of an special session of parliament called to debate the bank sale.
Bank Austria has put up most cash for the privatisation with 17.1 billion schillings ($1.6 billion) and its victory in the seven-year privatisation looked a sure bet.

Far-right leader Joerg Haider, eager to make political capital out a government split, has said the vote of his nationalist Freedom Party in parliament depended on Creditanstalt's small shareholders getting a fair deal out of the privatisation.

The conservatives, backed by Haider, want to ensure small shareholders receive the same price per share as the 861 schillings Bank Austria has offered, considerably more than the bank's Friday share value of 720.5.

The People's Party and the nationalist far right, which captured nearly 28 percent of the vote in European elections last October, can command a majority in parliament and could outvote the Social Democrats -- a result which could seriously endanger the survival of the one-year government.

In an atmosphere of recrimination, senior members of the erstwhile coalition partners traded insults before the talks began. Schuessel indirectly called for the resignation of Social Democrat chief whip Peter Kostelka over offensive comments he made about the conservatives.
In the some of the strongest language used in the coalition row, People's Party chief whip Andreas Khol said Vranitzky's style made him "want to vomit".
